faqs.q: How long does a shake roof last in West Orange?

runs.v: A shake roof lasts 20 to 40 years, per the CSSB, against the single "Wood" service life of 25 years on the InterNACHI chart, while many roofs typically last 15 to 20 years before needing repairs. Moisture management sets the lifespan, because the shakes need at least 1.5 inches of underside air space, and the reservation-edge canopy off South Mountain and Eagle Rock shades slopes that degrade faster.

faqs.q: Can individual shakes be repaired without replacing the whole roof?

runs.v: Yes, when cupping and splitting stay under 25 to 30% of the shakes and the deck stays sound; full replacement is favored above that share or with deck decay across more than 15% of the roof area, per CSSB and industry guidance. Roof repairs can address a leak, shingle damage, missing shingles, and storm issues, and roof repair services on a shake roof swap out the damaged pieces one at a time.

faqs.q: Does a shake roof meet New Jersey fire code on a wooded West Orange lot?

runs.v: Pressure-impregnated fire-retardant shakes carry a Class B or Class C fire rating, while untreated shakes are nonclassified, and a Class A wood roof is reached only as an assembly of Class B fire-retardant shakes over a fire-retardant cap sheet, per UL 790 and ASTM E108 testing under the CSSB Certi-Guard program. Every shake the crew lays is graded to CSSB standards.

faqs.q: Does a shake roof on a West Orange historic landmark need extra approval?

runs.v: It can: confirm with the West Orange construction office before work, since properties in a historic district or on a local landmark list can need extra review. Per the National Park Service, National Register listing alone places no federal restriction on a private property owner.

faqs.q: Do you need a permit for a shake roof in West Orange, NJ?

runs.v: A shake re-roof of the roof covering on a detached one- or two-family home counts as ordinary maintenance under N.J.A.C. 5:23-2.7 and requires no construction permit, while a commercial, multi-family, or attached roof, or any structural change, does require one, per the NJ Uniform Construction Code. The NJ Rehabilitation Subcode requires complete removal of a wood-shake covering rather than a recover-over, per N.J.A.C. 5:23-6.4.
